subject: Discovery recap — p95 latency & streaming concurrency (Finly)
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
To: Tom Harris <tharris@finly.com>, Elena Ruiz <elena.ruiz@finly.com>
Cc: Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.com>
Date: Sat, 12 Sep 2026 15:05:00 -0700
Subject: Discovery recap — p95 latency & streaming concurrency (Finly)

Hi Tom / Elena —

Thanks again for the call today. Quick recap of what we captured and the proposed next steps so we’re all aligned.

Pain points we heard
- Customer-facing chat experiences feel sluggish for long-form generation; product team sees a 1.6–2.1s p95 for typical billing-summary prompts today.
- Streaming UX is inconsistent: first-byte delays and chunking behaviour are causing perceived lag.
- Peak concurrency spikes during morning batch runs and EBITDA reporting windows — team estimates ~60–80 concurrent live chat sessions at peak.

Current stack (as discussed)
- Frontend: React web chat, websocket streaming.
- Backend: GCP region (us-west1), internal inference service running an open 7B LLM on shared GPU fleet; no prefix cache, rudimentary batching.

Success criteria (what Finly needs this project to achieve)
- P95 end-to-end generation latency <= 500ms for common single-turn flows (500–800 token outputs) to meet product UX targets.
- Reliable streaming first-byte < 200ms and smooth incremental token delivery.
- Support sustained concurrency of 75 concurrent streaming sessions with graceful degradation (fallback to smaller model if needed).

Suggested next steps
1) Technical deep-dive with Aditya (solutions engineering) to review model size variants, batching, caching, and kernel trade-offs — proposed week of Sep 15.
2) Share current p95 traces and a small sample traffic dump (anonymized) — I attached a template and the proposed Finly p95 worksheet.
3) Draft a mutual action plan (timeline, milestones, success metrics) — I’ll send a short M-AP after the deep-dive.

Attachments: redwood-discovery-deck.pdf (short deck), finly-p95-requirements.xlsx (worksheet template).

If anything above doesn’t match your notes, flag it and I’ll update. Otherwise I’ll get Aditya looped in to schedule the deep-dive.

Best,

Marissa Cole
Account Executive | Redwood Inference
marissa_cole@redwood.com
+1 (415) 555-0198

Subject: Re: Discovery recap — p95 latency & streaming concurrency (Finly)

Thanks Marissa — this looks correct and helpful. A few clarifications from our side that will help the deep-dive:

- Current p95 numbers: for 512–1024 token responses we’re seeing ~1.8s p95 on average; the worst-case long prompts (2k tokens) spike to ~3.5s.
- Concurrency: our production peaks are around 75 active streaming sessions, but we want headroom to 100 for growth.
- Streaming UX: primary complaint is first-byte variability. We need consistent first-byte under 200ms for eligibility in our in-app “instant” experience.
- Resilience: any solution should support model fallback with minimal session disruption; the product team wants an A/B plan to evaluate quality regressions.

For the deep-dive, please include: kernel/quantization options, autoscaling behavior for burst traffic, prefix/KV cache feasibility, and an example config that would meet the p95 targets.

We’re good to meet next week — Tue or Wed morning PT works for Elena and me.

- Tom
Director of Product, Finly
tharris@finly.com

From: Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.com>

Date: Sun, 13 Sep 2026 11:20:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Discovery recap — p95 latency & streaming concurrency (Finly)

Marissa — quick internal note before I join the deep-dive.

Notes from my side:
- Likely technical levers: 1) smaller model with aggressive quantization + prefix cache; 2) streaming tuning to push first-byte earlier (kernel-level prefetch and lower emit latency); 3) adaptive batching by client latency SLOs (avoid large batches for interactive flows).
- For 500ms p95 on 800-token outputs at ~75 concurrency we should target: per-request compute ~200–300ms, network and serialization <150ms, buffer for spikes. This maps to either optimized 13B on A100 or quantized 7B on Ampere-class instances with KV cache.
- Action items for deep-dive: request anonymized traces, traffic shape (token distribution), and a current infra summary (instance types, autoscale knobs).

I’ll join the Tue slot and bring a short checklist + config examples to test during PoC.

— Aditya
